doc_summary: Bowman presents a human-moderated AI-AI debate agenda for scalable oversight of truthfulness, with results on QuALITY, LLM debaters, and the new GPQA testbed. He emphasizes reliability over coverage, adversarial setups, and candid discussion of failure modes like human judge blind spots.

items.claim: prefers precision over recall (trusting answers only when they resolve confidently) over answering every question because an elicited answer is only useful if it can be trusted to be correct.
items.quote: we're aiming for this kind of precision over recall case, where we're content if many of these debates don't resolve as long as when they do resolve, the judge is getting it right.

items.claim: prefers testbeds with a verified, clear expertise gap (questions unanswerable by skilled non-experts even with search) over datasets where shortcuts or web access can substitute for the capability being tested because otherwise the test does not measure reliance on the system.
items.quote: if you take this question and give it to a physicist, that they'll do quite poorly, even if they spend half an hour, or 45 minutes, and they're googling frantically and skimming scientific papers

items.claim: Validate that a task really requires the target capability by checking that shallow strategies (keyword search, skimming, brief access) fail, so results can't be explained by shortcuts.
items.quote: we verified that these questions can't be answered by someone who hasn't read the story. If you give someone the question and they sort of get brief access to the story for a minute, they can search through.

items.claim: Distrusts testbeds that leak or collapse (web-available stories, debaters quoting the entire story) because they let the judge bypass the thing being tested and require artificial patches like blocking internet access.
items.quote: QuALITY is also arguing about science fiction stories that are available on the web. So we also need to block internet access for our judges, which is not the setting we ultimately want to be in.

items.claim: prefers redundant safeguards (a high-confidence resolution requirement plus an adversarial opponent) over relying on a single mechanism like human verification because human reasoning is fallible.
items.quote: we would be relying very, very heavily on human reasoning being robust and reliable, infallible in a way that I am not thrilled about relying on.

items.claim: prefers assuming model motives are alien and possibly adversarial (so using adversarial evidence systems) over assuming cooperative honest behavior as in peer review because we can't trust a model's stated position reflects its beliefs.
items.quote: We're sort of assuming that a lot of the motivations behind the system are somewhat alien. That I think puts us in a position that is more similar to something like a criminal trial where everyone's motives are somewhat suspect

items.claim: Treat qualitative transcript realism under heavier optimization as a sign of life, alongside quantitative metrics like judge accuracy and ELO.
items.quote: qualitatively, as you optimize harder, the transcripts look more like sensible debates that are arguing about real considerations and real evidence. So that's an encouraging sign of life.

items.claim: Report positive results alongside candid caveats (residual 6-7% confident errors, no low-hanging fruit), calibrating claims to 'seems like it's working' rather than 'solved'.
items.quote: There's still 6% or 7% of these questions where the human judge confidently resolved in favor of the wrong answer. So there isn't low hanging fruit to make this really robust.

items.claim: Start with humans in all roles when models aren't yet capable enough to make the experiment interesting, then move to LLMs as capabilities arrive.
items.quote: our first efforts in this area were actually using humans instead of language models as the debaters because language models weren't quite reliable enough to be interesting.

items.claim: Open problem: whether judges trained on checkable domains transfer to harder, more alien domains, plus whether human blind spots can be trained out.
items.quote: we're going to train our judges really extensively on all kinds of domains where we can check the answer... and then have them try it out in a domain that is significantly harder and more alien. And we'd like good proxies for that.

items.claim: Explicitly names conditions under which the approach fails (irreducibly complex arguments, systematic human blind spots) and says to abandon reliance if they hold.
items.quote: if there are cases like that where just there are sort of deep vulnerabilities in human reasoning, then none of this works. We shouldn't rely on it.
